{{Short description|Research study variability considered during meta-analytic, systematic reviews}}
In [[statistics]], '''(between-) study heterogeneity''' is a phenomenon that commonly occurs when attempting to undertake a [[meta-analysis]]. In a simplistic scenario, studies whose results are to be combined in the meta-analysis would all be undertaken in the same way and to the same experimental protocols. Differences between outcomes would only be due to [[measurement error]] (and studies would hence be ''[[Homogeneity (statistics)|homogeneous]]''). Study heterogeneity denotes the [[variability (statistics)|variability]] in outcomes that goes beyond what would be expected (or could be explained) due to measurement error alone.<ref name="CochraneChapter10">{{Citation | last1=Deeks | first1=J.J. | last2=Higgins | first2=J.P.T. | last3=Altman | first3=D.G. | chapter=10.10 Heterogeneity | chapter-url=https://training.cochrane.org/handbook/current/chapter-10#section-10-10 | editor1-last=Higgins | editor1-first=J.P.T. | editor2-last=Thomas | editor2-first=J. | editor3-last=Chandler | editor3-first=J. | editor4-last=Cumpston | editor4-first=M. | editor5-last=Li | editor5-first=T. | editor6-last=Page | editor6-first=M.J. | editor7-last=Welch | editor7-first=V.A. | title=Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions | edition=6.2 | year=2021 | url=https://training.cochrane.org/handbook}}</ref>

==Introduction==

[[Meta-analysis]] is a method used to combine the results of different trials in order to obtain a quantitative synthesis. The size of individual clinical trials is often too small to detect treatment effects reliably. Meta-analysis increases the power of statistical analyses by pooling the results of all available trials.

As one tries to use meta-analysis to estimate a combined effect from a group of similar studies, the effects found in the individual studies need to be similar enough that one can be confident that a combined estimate will be a meaningful description of the set of studies. However, the individual estimates of treatment effect will vary by chance; some variation is expected due to [[observational error]]. Any excess variation (whether it is apparent or detectable or not) is called [[Homogeneity_and_heterogeneity_(statistics)|(statistical) heterogeneity]].<ref>{{Citation | last1=Singh | first1=A. | last2=Hussain | first2=S. | last3=Najmi | first3=A.N. | title=Number of studies, heterogeneity, generalisability, and the choice of method for meta-analysis | journal=Journal of the Neurological Sciences | year=2017 | volume=15 | issue=381 | page=347 | doi=10.1016/j.jns.2017.09.026| pmid=28967410 | s2cid=31073171 }}</ref>
The presence of some heterogeneity is not unusual, e.g., analogous effects are also commonly encountered even ''within'' studies, in [[multicenter trial]]s  (between-''center'' heterogeneity).

Reasons for the additional variability are usually differences in the studies themselves, the investigated populations, treatment schedules, endpoint definitions, or other circumstances ("clinical diversity"), or the way data were analyzed, what models were employed, or whether estimates have been adjusted in some way ("methodological diversity").<ref name="CochraneChapter10" /> Different types of [[effect size|effect measures]] (e.g., [[odds ratio]] vs. [[relative risk]]) may also be more or less susceptible to heterogeneity.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Deeks | first1=J.J. | author2-link=Doug Altman | last2=Altman | first2=D.G. | chapter=Effect measures for meta-analysis of trials with binary outcomes | editor-last1=Egger | editor-first1=M. | editor-last2=Davey Smith | editor-first2=G. | editor-last3=Altman | editor-first3=D. | title=Systematic reviews in health care: Meta-analysis in context | year=2001 | edition=2nd | publisher=BMJ Publishing | pages=313–335 | doi=10.1002/9780470693926.ch16| isbn=978-0-470-69392-6 }}</ref>

==Modeling==

In case the origin of heterogeneity can be identified and may be attributed to certain study features, the analysis may be [[stratification (clinical trials)|stratified]] (by considering subgroups of studies, which would then hopefully be more homogeneous), or by extending the analysis to a [[meta-regression]], accounting for (continuous or [[categorical variable|categorical]]) [[moderator variable]]s. Unfortunately, literature-based meta-analysis may often not allow for gathering data on all (potentially) relevant moderators.<ref>{{Cite book|last1=Cooper|first1=Harris|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=tfeXDwAAQBAJ&dq=The+Handbook+of+research+synthesis+and+meta-analysis&pg=PR5|title=The Handbook of Research Synthesis and Meta-Analysis|last2=Hedges|first2=Larry V.|last3=Valentine|first3=Jeffrey C.|date=2019-06-14|publisher=Russell Sage Foundation|isbn=978-1-61044-886-4|language=en}}</ref>

In addition, heterogeneity is usually accommodated by using a [[random effects model]], in which the heterogeneity then constitutes a [[variance component]].<ref name="RileyEtAl2011">{{Citation | last1=Riley | first1=R. D. | last2=Higgins | first2=J. P. | last3=Deeks | first3=J. J. | title= Interpretation of random-effects meta-analyses | journal=BMJ | volume=342 | pages=d549 | year=2011 | doi= 10.1136/bmj.d549 | pmid=21310794| s2cid=32994689 }}</ref> The model represents the lack of knowledge about why treatment effects may differ by treating the (potential) differences as unknowns. The centre of this symmetric distribution describes the average of the effects, while its width describes the degree of heterogeneity. The obvious and conventional choice of distribution is a [[normal distribution]]. It is difficult to establish the validity of any distributional assumption, and this is a common criticism of random effects meta-analyses. However, variations of the exact distributional form may not make much of a difference,<ref>{{Citation | last=Bretthorst | first=G.L. | chapter=The near-irrelevance of sampling frequency distributions | title=Maximum Entropy and Bayesian methods | pages=21–46 | publisher=Kluwer Academic Publishers | year = 1999 | editor-last1=von der Linden | editor-first1=W. | editor-last2=Dose | editor-first2=V. | display-editors=1 | doi=10.1007/978-94-011-4710-1_3| isbn=978-94-010-5982-4 }}</ref> and simulations have shown that methods are relatively robust even under extreme distributional assumptions, both in estimating heterogeneity,<ref name=KontopantelisP1>{{Cite journal | last1 = Kontopantelis | first1 = E. | last2 = Springate | first2 = D. A. | last3 = Reeves | first3 = D. | title = A re-analysis of the Cochrane Library data: The dangers of unobserved heterogeneity in meta-analyses | doi = 10.1371/journal.pone.0069930 | journal = PLOS ONE | volume = 8 | issue = 7 | article-number = e69930 | year = 2013 | pmid =  23922860| pmc =3724681 | bibcode = 2013PLoSO...869930K | doi-access = free }}</ref> and calculating an overall effect size.<ref name=KontopantelisSMMR10>{{Cite journal | last1 = Kontopantelis | first1 = E. | last2 = Reeves | first2 = D. | doi = 10.1177/0962280210392008| title = Performance of statistical methods for meta-analysis when true study effects are non-normally distributed: A simulation study. | journal = Statistical Methods in Medical Research | volume = 21 | issue = 4 | pages = 409–26| year = 2012 | pmid =  21148194| s2cid = 152379 | url = https://www.research.manchester.ac.uk/portal/en/publications/performance-of-statistical-methods-for-metaanalysis-when-true-study-effects-are-nonnormally-distributed-a-simulation-study(2634dc5c-0dbe-47d2-83ce-d58277108743).html }}</ref>

Inclusion of a [[random effect]] to the model has the effect of making the inferences (in a sense) more conservative or cautious, as a (non-zero) heterogeneity will lead to greater uncertainty (and avoid overconfidence) in the estimation of overall effects. In the special case of a zero heterogeneity variance, the random-effects model again reduces to the special case of the [[fixed effects model|common-effect]] model.<ref name="Roever2020">{{Citation | last=Röver | first=C. | title= Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis using the bayesmeta R package | journal=Journal of Statistical Software | volume=93 | issue=6 | pages=1–51 | year=2020 | doi=10.18637/jss.v093.i06| doi-access=free | arxiv=1711.08683 }}</ref>

Common meta-analysis models, however, should, of course, not be applied blindly or naively to collected sets of estimates. In case the results to be amalgamated differ substantially (in their contexts or in their estimated effects), a derived meta-analytic average may eventually not correspond to a reasonable [[estimand]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Cornell|first1=John E.|last2=Mulrow|first2=Cynthia D.|last3=Localio|first3=Russell|last4=Stack|first4=Catharine B.|last5=Meibohm|first5=Anne R.|last6=Guallar|first6=Eliseo|last7=Goodman|first7=Steven N.|date=2014-02-18|title=Random-Effects Meta-analysis of Inconsistent Effects: A Time for Change|url=https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/abs/10.7326/M13-2886|journal=Annals of Internal Medicine|volume=160|issue=4|pages=267–270|doi=10.7326/M13-2886|pmid=24727843|s2cid=9210956|issn=0003-4819|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Maziarz|first=Mariusz|date=2022-02-01|title=Is meta-analysis of RCTs assessing the efficacy of interventions a reliable source of evidence for therapeutic decisions?|journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science|language=en|volume=91|pages=159–167|doi=10.1016/j.shpsa.2021.11.007|pmid=34922183|s2cid=245241150|issn=0039-3681|doi-access=free}}</ref>
When individual studies exhibit conflicting results, there likely are some reasons why the results differ; for instance, two subpopulations may experience different [[Pharmacokinetics|pharmacokinetic pathways]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Borenstein|first1=Michael|last2=Hedges|first2=Larry V.|last3=Higgins|first3=Julian P. T.|last4=Rothstein|first4=Hannah R.|date=2010|title=A basic introduction to fixed-effect and random-effects models for meta-analysis|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/jrsm.12|journal=Research Synthesis Methods|language=en|volume=1|issue=2|pages=97–111|doi=10.1002/jrsm.12|pmid=26061376|s2cid=1040498 |issn=1759-2887|url-access=subscription}}</ref> In such a scenario, it would be important to both know ''and'' consider relevant covariables in an analysis.

==Testing==

Statistical testing for a non-zero heterogeneity variance is often done based on ''[[William Gemmell Cochran|Cochran]]'s Q''<ref>{{Citation | last=Cochran | first=W.G. | title=The combination of estimates from different experiments | journal=Biometrics | year=1954 | volume=10 | issue=1 | pages=101–129 | doi=10.2307/3001666| jstor=3001666 }}</ref> or related test procedures. This common procedure however is questionable for several reasons, namely, the low [[power of a test|power]] of such tests<ref>{{Citation | last1=Hardy | first1=R.J. | last2=Thompson | first2=S.G. | title=Detecting and describing heterogeneity in meta-analysis | journal=Statistics in Medicine | year=1998 | volume=17 | issue=8 | pages=841–856 | doi=10.1002/(SICI)1097-0258(19980430)17:8<841::AID-SIM781>3.0.CO;2-D | pmid=9595615 }}</ref> especially in the very common case of only few estimates being combined in the analysis,<ref>{{Citation | last1=Davey | first1=J. | last2=Turner | first2=R.M. | last3=Clarke | first3=M.J. | last4=Higgins | first4=J.P.T. | title=Characteristics of meta-analyses and their component studies in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews: a cross-sectional, descriptive analysis | journal=BMC Medical Research Methodology | year=2011 | volume=11 | issue=1 | page=160 | doi=10.1186/1471-2288-11-160| pmid=22114982 | pmc=3247075 | doi-access=free }}</ref><ref name="KontopantelisP1" /> as well as the specification of ''homogeneity'' as the [[null hypothesis]] which is then only rejected in the presence of sufficient evidence against it.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Li | first1=W. | last2=Liu | first2=F. | last3=Snavely | first3=D. | title=Revisit of test-then-pool methods and some practical considerations | journal=Pharmaceutical Statistics | volume=19 | issue=5 | pages=498–517 | year=2020 | doi=10.1002/pst.2009| pmid=32171048 | s2cid=212718520 }}</ref>

==Estimation==

While the main purpose of a meta-analysis usually is estimation of the ''main effect'', investigation of the ''heterogeneity'' is also crucial for its interpretation. A large number of ([[frequentist]] and [[Bayesian inference|Bayesian]]) [[estimator]]s is available.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Veroniki | first1=A.A. | last2=Jackson | first2=D. | last3=Viechtbauer | first3=W. | last4=Bender | first4=R. | last5=Bowden | first5=J. | last6=Knapp | first6=G. | last7=Kuß | first7=O. | last8=Higgins | first8=J.P.T. | last9=Langan | first9=D. | last10=Salanti | first10=G. | year=2016 | title=Methods to estimate the between-study variance and its uncertainty in meta-analysis | journal=Research Synthesis Methods | volume=7 | issue=1 | pages=55–79 | doi=10.1002/jrsm.1164| pmid=26332144 | pmc=4950030 | doi-access=free }}</ref> Bayesian estimation of the heterogeneity usually requires the specification of an appropriate [[prior probability distribution|prior distribution]].<ref name="Roever2020" /><ref name="RoeverEtAl2020">{{Citation | last1=Röver | first1=C. | last2=Bender | first2=R. | last3=Dias | first3=S. | last4=Schmid | first4=C.H. | last5=Schmidli | first5=H. | last6=Sturtz | first6=S. | last7=Weber | first7=S. | last8=Friede | first8=T. | title=On weakly informative prior distributions for the heterogeneity parameter in Bayesian random-effects meta-analysis | journal=Research Synthesis Methods | year=2021 | volume=12 | issue=4 | pages=448–474 | doi=10.1002/jrsm.1475 | pmid=33486828 | arxiv=2007.08352| s2cid=220546288 }}</ref>

While many of these estimators behave similarly in case of a large number of studies, differences in particular arise in their behaviour in the common case of only few estimates.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Friede | first1=T. | last2=Röver | first2=C. | last3=Wandel | first3=S. | last4=Neuenschwander | first4=B. | title=Meta-analysis of few small studies in orphan diseases | year=2017 | journal=Research Synthesis Methods | volume=8 | issue=1 | pages=79–91 | doi=10.1002/jrsm.1217 | pmid=27362487 | pmc=5347842 | arxiv=1601.06533}}</ref> An incorrect zero between-study variance estimate is frequently obtained, leading to a false homogeneity assumption. Overall, it appears that heterogeneity is being consistently underestimated in meta-analyses.<ref name=KontopantelisP1/>

==Quantification==

The heterogeneity ''[[variance]]'' is commonly denoted by τ², or the [[standard deviation]] (its square root) by τ. Heterogeneity is probably most readily interpretable in terms of τ, as this is the heterogeneity distribution's [[scale parameter]], which is measured in the same [[unit of measurement|units]] as the overall effect itself.<ref name="RoeverEtAl2020" />

Another common measure of heterogeneity is ''I''², a statistic that indicates the ''percentage of variance'' in a meta-analysis that is attributable to study heterogeneity (somewhat similarly to a [[coefficient of determination]]).<ref name=HigginsBMJ03>{{Citation| last1 = Higgins | first1 = J. P. T. | last2 = Thompson | first2 = S. G. | last3 = Deeks | first3 = J. J. | last4 = Altman | first4 = D. G. | title = Measuring inconsistency in meta-analyses | doi = 10.1136/bmj.327.7414.557 | journal = BMJ | volume = 327 | issue = 7414 | pages = 557–560 | year = 2003 | pmid = 12958120 | pmc =192859 }}</ref>
''I''² relates the heterogeneity variance's magnitude to the size of the individual estimates' variances (squared [[standard error]]s); with this normalisation however, it is not quite obvious what exactly would constitute "small" or "large" amounts of heterogeneity. For a constant heterogeneity (τ), the availability of smaller or larger studies (with correspondingly differing standard errors associated) would affect the ''I''² measure; so the actual interpretation of an ''I''² value is not straightforward.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Rücker | first1=G. | last2=Schwarzer | first2=G. | last3=Carpenter | first3=J.R. | last4=Schumacher | first4=M. | year=2008 | title=Undue reliance on ''I''² in assessing heterogeneity may mislead | journal=BMC Medical Research Methodology | volume=8 | issue=79 | page=79 | doi=10.1186/1471-2288-8-79| pmid=19036172 | pmc=2648991 | doi-access=free }}</ref>
<ref>{{Citation | last1=Borenstein | first1=M. | last2=Higgins | first2=J.P.T. | last3=Hedges | first3=L.V. | last4=Rothstein | first4=H.R. | year=2017 | title=Basics of meta-analysis: ''I''² is not an absolute measure of heterogeneity | journal=Research Synthesis Methods | volume=8 | issue=1 | pages=5–18 | doi=10.1002/jrsm.1230| pmid=28058794 | hdl=1983/9cea2307-8e9b-4583-9403-3a37409ed1cb | s2cid=4235538 | url=https://research-information.bris.ac.uk/ws/files/88672054/Final_I_squared_paper_full.pdf | hdl-access=free }}</ref>

The joint consideration of a ''prediction interval'' along with a [[confidence interval]] for the main effect may help getting a better sense of the contribution of heterogeneity to the uncertainty around the effect estimate.<ref  name="RileyEtAl2011" /><ref>{{Citation | last1=Chiolero | first1=A |last2=Santschi | first2=V. | last3=Burnand | first3=B. | last4=Platt | first4=R.W. | last5=Paradis | first5=G. | title=Meta-analyses: with confidence or prediction intervals? | journal=European Journal of Epidemiology | year=2012 | volume=27 | issue=10 | pages=823–5 | pmid=23070657 | doi=10.1007/s10654-012-9738-y| s2cid=20413290 | url=http://doc.rero.ch/record/320413/files/10654_2012_Article_9738.pdf }}</ref><ref>{{Citation | last1=Bender | first1=R. | last2=Kuß | first2=O. | last3=Koch | first3=A. | last4=Schwenke | first4=C. | last5=Hauschke | first5=D. | title=Application of prediction intervals in meta-analyses with random effects | publisher=Joint statement of [[IQWiG]], GMDS and [[International Biometric Society|IBS-DR]] | year=2014 | url=https://www.iqwig.de/download/2014-03-07_Joint_Statement_Prediction_Intervals.pdf}}</ref><ref>{{Citation | last1=IntHout | first1=J |last2=Ioannidis | first2=J.P.A. | last3=Rovers | first3=M.M. | last4=Goeman | first4=J.J. | title=Plea for routinely presenting prediction intervals in meta-analysis | journal=BMJ Open | year=2016 | volume=6 | issue=7 | article-number=e010247 | pmid=27406637 | doi=10.1136/bmjopen-2015-010247 | pmc=4947751 |url=https://bmjopen.bmj.com/content/bmjopen/6/7/e010247.full.pdf |doi-access=free }}</ref>
